convention: Every case of the readers' tests in which a reader reads a text otherwise than its language does and that is not yet mended, listed under its cause: what the reader reads, what is true and by what source, and how many places the corpora hold (a plain search over the corpora of 2026-11-21, dnn, mojoportal, dbatools, tsqlt, algo, azurestack, eshoponweb, nopcommerce and orchardcore, unless the cause says the independent reviewer of that day counted it). A test runs each case through heldToLedger (knownDifferences.ts): a listed case that passes fails, so a mend takes it out of the ledger in the same change, and a failing case this ledger does not list fails. Each case is `<test file> > <the test's full name>`. Every cause here waits on one of two designs, measured before it is built: a dialect for each SQL script, or a markup reader that reads the code a page holds by that code's own parse (2026-11-21, the second review that broke the comment guard by new means).

causes.cause: SQL, PostgreSQL's schema public: the reader takes PUBLIC for T-SQL's reserved word, so `CREATE TABLE public.t` declares nothing and `FROM public.t` names nothing.
causes.truth: PostgreSQL reserves no `public`; its default schema is named so (PostgreSQL's "The Public Schema"), and pg_dump writes it before every name.
causes.corpora: The reviewer counted mojoPortal's 13 PostgreSQL install scripts: 0 declarations, 517 when the schema is written quoted; a plain search finds `public.` before a name 100 times in 3 files.
cases: openings.test.ts > database objects in PostgreSQL's and MySQL's spellings > reads a name in PostgreSQL's schema `public`

causes.cause: SQL, PostgreSQL's dollar-quoted strings: the reader lexes `$$ … $$` as SQL, so an apostrophe in it opens a string that runs on, and a function's body, a dollar-quoted string, is read as statements.
causes.truth: PostgreSQL's "Dollar-Quoted String Constants": "no characters inside a dollar-quoted string are ever escaped"; the body is one string.
causes.corpora: A plain search finds a dollar quote 160 times in 8 .sql files (mojoPortal's PostgreSQL scripts).
cases: openings.test.ts > database objects in PostgreSQL's and MySQL's spellings > reads past a dollar-quoted string that holds an apostrophe

causes.cause: SQL, a module's body read by T-SQL's rule: a PostgreSQL function and a MySQL procedure are taken to run to the end of their batch, which a script of either never marks, so every table after them is taken for one their body makes.
causes.truth: PostgreSQL's CREATE FUNCTION ends at its statement's end, the body being a string; MySQL's CREATE PROCEDURE ends with its one body statement, `BEGIN … END`, which the client's DELIMITER lets hold `;`.
causes.corpora: A plain search finds no `DELIMITER` in the corpora's .sql files; the PostgreSQL functions are among the 160 dollar quotes above.
cases: openings.test.ts > database objects in PostgreSQL's and MySQL's spellings > ends a PostgreSQL function at the end of its statement, not of the script
openings.test.ts > database objects in PostgreSQL's and MySQL's spellings > reads MySQL's `CREATE DEFINER=… PROCEDURE`, and ends a procedure at its body's `END`

causes.cause: SQL, PostgreSQL's and Oracle's materialized view: `MATERIALIZED` is no word the reader passes over, so the view is not declared.
causes.truth: PostgreSQL's "CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW" makes a lasting view whose rows are kept.
causes.corpora: A plain search finds none in the corpora.
cases: openings.test.ts > database objects in PostgreSQL's and MySQL's spellings > reads a materialized view as a view

causes.cause: SQL, MySQL's comments: `#` to the line's end, which the reader reads as the start of T-SQL's temporary name, and `/*! … */`, which MySQL runs and the reader drops.
causes.truth: MySQL's "Comments": "From a # character to the end of the line"; "/*! MySQL-specific code */ … MySQL Server parses and executes the code within the comment".
causes.corpora: A plain search finds a `#` comment line once in 1 .sql file and no `/*!`.
cases: openings.test.ts > database objects in PostgreSQL's and MySQL's spellings > reads nothing after MySQL's `#` comment
openings.test.ts > database objects in PostgreSQL's and MySQL's spellings > reads what MySQL's executable comment holds, as mysqldump writes a view

causes.cause: SQL, MySQL's backslash-escaped quote: the reader ends a string at `\'`, as T-SQL does in `'C:\Backup\'`, so the string runs on.
causes.truth: MySQL's "String Literals": `\'` is a single quote unless NO_BACKSLASH_ESCAPES.
causes.corpora: A plain search finds `\'` twice in 1 .sql file.
cases: openings.test.ts > database objects in PostgreSQL's and MySQL's spellings > reads past MySQL's backslash-escaped quote

causes.cause: SQL, SQLite's own rules: its block comments do not nest, `temp.x` is its temporary schema, and `key`, `file` and `user` are names it makes tables of, where T-SQL nests comments, `temp` is a schema like any and those words are reserved.
causes.truth: SQLite itself, run on each script in the test (`runSqlite`); SQLite's "Comments": "Comments do not nest".
causes.corpora: A plain search finds no `CREATE TABLE temp.` in the corpora; the other two not counted.

sqlite-oracle.test.ts > the SQL reader against SQLite, on scripts SQLite runs here > declares what SQLite makes of reserved.sql

causes.cause: Markup, a `<noscript>`'s text: the reader reads it as markup, so a `<!--` in it opens a comment that hides what follows.
causes.truth: WHATWG HTML, "noscript": with scripting enabled the parser reads its content as raw text, in which `<!--` opens nothing; without scripting it is markup, so the rule depends on the browser.
causes.corpora: A plain search finds no `<!--` inside a `<noscript>` in the corpora's markup.

causes.cause: Markup, the server's own code in a page: the ASP.NET reader reads a Razor code block (`@{ … }`) and a Web Forms code block (`<% … %>`) as markup, so a C# comment there is read, a `<!--` in a C# string opens a comment, and Razor's escaped `@@*` opens a Razor comment.
causes.truth: The page parser hands those blocks to C#, where `//` and `/* */` are comments and `"<!--"` a string (C#'s lexical grammar); Razor's "To escape an @ symbol in Razor markup, use a second @ symbol".
causes.corpora: A plain search finds at most 444 Razor code blocks holding `//` or `/*` in 440 files (the search counts a `//` in a URL too), `@@` 33 times in 8 files, and no `<!--` or `-->` in a code block's string.

causes.cause: PowerShell, an expandable here-string holding `<#` or `#>`: the engine's grammar reads them as a block comment's ends, so what lies between two such here-strings is read as a comment.
causes.truth: PowerShell's own parser (pwsh 7.7.0, `[Parser]::ParseInput`) reads the here-strings' text as literal and finds the dot-source between them, with no parse error; a literal here-string (`@' … '@`) the grammar reads right. The grammar's fault, to be patched in `packages/engine/grammars/powershell` with corpus tests.
causes.corpora: A plain search finds `<#` or `#>` inside an expandable here-string 3 times in 2 files.
